steps.title: What this tool answers
steps.text:
We will work one question through: how wrong is the textbook resolution formula for my objective?

Everyone quotes 0.51 λ/NA. At the high NA people actually use, it is optimistic — and by how much depends on the polarization, which the formula does not mention at all. Six steps and you will have the number for your own optics.

steps.title: Step 1 — set your objective's NA
steps.text:
Type the NA of the objective you actually use. 1.40 is a common oil immersion value and is what the rest of this tour assumes.

The NA is what decides whether any of this matters: below about 1.0 the scalar formula is fine, and above it the field starts tipping out of the transverse plane.

steps.title: Step 2 — the immersion medium
steps.text:
Set n (immersion) to match: 1.518 for oil, 1.33 for water, 1.0 for air.

This is not decoration. The aperture half-angle is arcsin(NA/n), so the immersion index sets how strongly the lens focuses — and the NA can never exceed it.

steps.title: Step 3 — pick the scalar model first, deliberately
steps.text:
Choose Airy (scalar) here.

We are going to get the textbook answer before the honest one, so the difference is yours rather than mine. Watch the summary line under the controls: it reports the measured lateral width beside the 0.51 λ/NA prediction.

steps.title: Step 4 — now switch to vectorial
steps.text:
Change the optical model to Vectorial (Richards–Wolf).

The summary's lateral width grows. At NA 1.4 and 520 nm the true circular-polarization width is about 210 nm where the scalar formula says 189 nm — the textbook number is optimistic by roughly 11%, before anything else goes wrong.

steps.title: Step 5 — the part the formula cannot express
steps.text:
Set Polarization to Linear x.

The focus is now longer in one direction than the other — about 250 nm across x against 179 nm across y. A resolution quoted as a single number is hiding a 40% difference between two axes. Try Azimuthal too: it is a doughnut with an exact zero on axis, which no scalar model can produce.

steps.title: Step 6 — make the state visible
steps.text:
Tick Polarization vectors.

Strokes appear on a ring above the focus, along the local field direction — parallel for linear, outward for radial, tangential for azimuthal. They are here because the effect on the focus is real but subtle to the eye, and you should be able to see which state produced a picture without reading the controls.

steps.title: Last — switch to Full before you quote a number
steps.text:
Everything so far ran on Preview, which evaluates the aperture integral at 60 points so editing stays responsive. Set Quality to Full (300 points) before taking a width you intend to publish or feed to a deconvolution.

Increase Planes and lower z step if you care about the axial width: the default sampling is coarse enough to quantize it.

steps.title: Take it with you — export the volume
steps.text:
Export on the toolbar writes the volume you are looking at.

NumPy (.npy) keeps full float precision and nothing else — the right choice for feeding a deconvolution or a simulation.
ImageJ TIFF (.tif) is a 32-bit stack carrying the voxel size, so it opens in ImageJ or Fiji already scaled in micrometres instead of counting pixels.

Export what you meant to export: the file records whatever is currently computed, so switch Quality to Full first.
